tier_reason: Upgraded from B. The report's numbers come from public Criterion code in DRMacIver/rust-bigint-benchmarks (benches/primitive.rs, small_int.rs, workload.rs, shrinker.rs; tables generated by scripts/gen_report.py), which runs dashu-int 0.4.2 and rug 1.30.0 (gmp-mpfr-sys 1.7.1, pinned in Cargo.lock) in one process. The page states rustc 1.92.0 and an Apple M2 Max, and Cargo.toml has no [profile] overrides, so `cargo bench` uses the default bench profile (opt-level 3); code, compiler, flags and CPU are all public, as in earlier default-release-build precedents.

corrections.baseline: GNU GMP (mpz, via the Rust rug 1.30.0 crate; gmp-mpfr-sys 1.7.1 pinned in Cargo.lock)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.92.0 (ded5c06cf 2025-12-08); cargo bench --features gmp with the default bench profile (Cargo.toml sets no [profile] overrides, so opt-level 3, inherits release); criterion 0.5.1 run with --warm-up-time 1 --measurement-time 2 --sample-size 100; dashu-int 0.4.2, rug 1.30.0 with gmp-mpfr-sys 1.7.1 (Cargo.lock)
corrections.claimed_speedup: Small operands: ubig_add at 100 bits dashu 3.7 ns vs rug 21.9 ns; ubig_div at 100 bits 5.7 ns vs 32.4 ns; ubig_mul at 100 bits 22.6 ns vs 25.1 ns; ubig_gcd at 1000 bits 2.87 us vs 3.05 us; ubig_from_hex at 10^4 bits 2.56 us vs 6.60 us. Report summary: dashu faster than rug in 98 of 153 small-value cases and in 123 of 205 head-to-head cases overall; the page says rug/GMP is typically 2-6x slower on tiny values because of a fixed per-value heap allocation. rug/GMP is faster from about 1000 bits (ubig_mul at 10^4 bits: rug 4.52 us vs dashu 12.76 us).
corrections.is_fork_of: https://github.com/tczajka/ibig-rs (hard fork: tczajka/bigint-benchmark-rs README lists dashu as 'Fork of ibig' and the DRMacIver README calls ibig 'dashu-int's ancestor'; not a GitHub fork)
corrections.stars_or_usage: 142 stars, 20 forks; dashu-int 3,894,865 crates.io downloads (1,662,908 recent) as of 2026-10-01
corrections.caveats: The report calls itself 'quick, machine-specific local numbers, not authoritative' (one laptop, 2 s measurement). It benchmarks dashu-int 0.4.2, while crates.io's current release is 0.6.1 (2026-09-25). Each bench op returns a new value, so rug pays a heap allocation per result while dashu stores up to two words inline; the small-value win is about allocation and inline storage, not GMP's mpn kernels. The ubig_div bench divides two operands of the same bit length (b = random + a), so the quotient is tiny and it measures overhead, not long division. The suite was written for (but not merged into) the dashu repo and generalises dashu's own primitive.rs bench, so it is not fully arm's-length. The bit-width sweep stops at 10^4 bits. A second suite by ibig's author (github.com/tczajka/bigint-benchmark-rs, rug 1.24.1, dashu 0.4.2) shows GMP-backed rug far ahead on large workloads: digits of e at 10M rug 2.788 s vs dashu 19.943 s; Fibonacci at 100M rug 2.937 s vs dashu 26.224 s. The win is limited to small operands (about two words) and gcd near 1000 bits.

notes: All claimed numbers are on the page in dashu's and rug's rows, and the second-suite numbers in the caveats match tczajka/bigint-benchmark-rs. Metadata checked: MIT OR Apache-2.0, not archived, not a GitHub fork, last commit 2026-09-30, 142 stars. Worth recording that the win is small-operand only and the measured version (0.4.2) is behind the current 0.6.1.

tier_reason: Upgraded from B. The same public Criterion suite (DRMacIver/rust-bigint-benchmarks benches/primitive.rs and small_int.rs; Ibig backend) runs ibig 0.3.6 and rug 1.30.0 (gmp-mpfr-sys 1.7.1, Cargo.lock) side by side. The page states rustc 1.92.0 and an Apple M2 Max, and Cargo.toml has no [profile] overrides (default bench profile, opt-level 3), so code, compiler, flags and CPU are all public.

corrections.baseline: GNU GMP (mpz, via the Rust rug 1.30.0 crate; gmp-mpfr-sys 1.7.1 pinned in Cargo.lock)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.92.0 (ded5c06cf 2025-12-08); cargo bench --features gmp with the default bench profile (Cargo.toml sets no [profile] overrides, so opt-level 3, inherits release); criterion 0.5.1 run with --warm-up-time 1 --measurement-time 2 --sample-size 100; ibig 0.3.6, rug 1.30.0 with gmp-mpfr-sys 1.7.1 (Cargo.lock)
corrections.claimed_speedup: At 10 bits: ubig_add ibig 1.8 ns vs rug 17.7 ns, ubig_sub 1.5 ns vs 18.0 ns, ubig_mul 2.1 ns vs 18.0 ns, ubig_div 1.5 ns vs 28.3 ns. Parsing beats rug at every size: ubig_from_hex at 10^4 bits 2.55 us vs 6.60 us, ubig_from_dec 10.17 us vs 11.51 us; ibig_from_str_small 34.1 ns vs 111.3 ns. Already at 100 bits rug wins add/sub/div (ubig_add 25.7 ns vs 21.9 ns), and at 10^4 bits GMP wins clearly: ubig_mul rug 4.52 us vs ibig 12.69 us.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 107 stars; ibig crate 875,051 crates.io downloads (118,046 recent) as of 2026-10-01; last crates.io release 0.3.6 (2022-09-17)
corrections.caveats: Win over GMP is confined to one-word integers (about 10 bits in the sweep) and to string parsing; from 100 bits rug is ahead on add/sub/div, and ibig's gcd is far slower than rug at every size from 100 bits (ubig_gcd at 10^4 bits 850.52 us vs 53.05 us). Each bench op returns a new value, so rug pays a heap allocation per result while ibig stores one word inline; the small-value win is about allocation, not GMP's kernels. The ubig_div bench divides equal-length operands (tiny quotient). The benchmarked crate is ibig 0.3.6, the last crates.io release (2022-09-17); the repository has since been restructured (ibig, ibig-core, ibig-old directories; rustc 1.95 MSRV), so current code may differ. In the second suite by ibig's own author (github.com/tczajka/bigint-benchmark-rs, rug 1.24.1) ibig is far behind rug on large workloads (digits of e at 10M: rug 2.788 s vs ibig 20.673 s). Dashu, a hard fork of ibig, is its own entry. The report calls itself non-authoritative (one laptop, 2 s measurement).

notes: Numbers verified in ibig's column of the shared report. Metadata checked: MIT OR Apache-2.0, not archived, not a fork, last commit 2026-07-24, 107 stars, MSRV 1.95 and ibig-old directory confirmed. The win is narrow (one-word values and parsing); the crate has had no release since 2022 even though the repo is active.

tier_reason: The libbeef report (by the author of a competing Rust port) puts libbf numbers from a locally built C bftest next to MPFR numbers from rug in a separate Rust harness, with different operand generators and unstated rounding mode. The public bftest.c (libbf 2025-06-03) times with x86 rdtsc, prints cycles per limb ('c/64bit') and has its own MPFR column on identical operands; the report says its C harness used clock_gettime on an Apple M4, so it was modified and the patch is not published, and the like-for-like MPFR column was not reported. A harness absent from public sources plus a cross-harness comparison gives C, not B.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: libbf 2025-06-03 bftest built locally with clang -O2 ('./bftest -S -p <prec> <op> <op>'); the report says the C harness timed with clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC), but the public bftest.c uses x86 rdtsc and prints cycles per limb, so the harness was modified (patch not published). MPFR side: rug 1.30.0 (gmp-mpfr-sys 1.7.1, GMP 6.3, MPFR 4.2) under rustc 1.96.1 --release in libbeef's tests/bftest.rs (BFTEST_SEED=1234, BFTEST_DURATION=200)
corrections.claimed_speedup: Multiplication at 300,000-bit precision: libbf 51.2 ns/limb vs MPFR (rug) 78.9 ns/limb (about 1.5x, derived from page data), from two different harnesses. libbf is slower than MPFR everywhere else on the page: mul at 53 bits 43.4 vs 15.6, 3,000 bits 13.0 vs 9.4, 30,000 bits 43.0 vs 35.3; add, div and sqrt at every size; and exp/log/sin/cos/tan/atan/pow at 53-256 bits (for example exp at 53 bits 2985 vs 518).
corrections.is_fork_of: https://bellard.org/libbf (mirror of Fabrice Bellard's libbf tar releases with fixes and CI; not a GitHub fork)
corrections.stars_or_usage: 19 stars (rurban/libbf mirror). It was QuickJS's BigInt/BigFloat backend until the QuickJS 2025-04-26 release removed the bignum extensions and added a new BigInt implementation; the current QuickJS Makefile no longer builds libbf.
corrections.caveats: The only win over MPFR is multiplication at 300,000 bits on one Apple M4, and it is not a like-for-like measurement: libbf ran in its own C bftest (operands of uniform random length in [1, 2*prec] bits with run-length random bits, results printed per rounding mode including RNDF, where bf_mul truncates inputs to prec+2 bits; the report does not say which line it quoted) while MPFR ran via rug in libbeef's Rust harness with full-width operands. The public bftest.c already prints an MPFR column on identical operands, which the report did not quote, and it times with x86 rdtsc (cycles), so the report's C harness on Apple M4 was an unpublished modification. Measured by the author of libbeef, a competing Rust port. libbf's own README says it 'is not the fastest library' and is about 4x slower than TachusPI on pi. bellard.org/libbf was blocked, so the GitHub mirror (rurban/libbf, last commit 2025-08-19) is cited.

notes: The page numbers match the record, but they do not show libbf faster than MPFR in any controlled comparison: the one winning cell is cross-harness and every other operation and size is slower. A 'not-faster' rejection would be defensible; I downgraded to C instead so it can be kept with that shortcoming recorded. Metadata: MIT, last commit 2025-08-19 (stale), 19 stars; QuickJS no longer uses libbf.
